title: BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A benchmark is laid out as staged components, from goals and taxonomies through datasets and harness to results, to support comparing systems under operational constraints.
layout: 6 numbered columns, left-to-right, chevron arrows, scatter plot in final column
description: The figure is a horizontal strip of six numbered gray cards, each with a title and an italic subtitle, linked by chevrons. 01 Goal contrasts specialized guardrails (blue dot) with generalist LLMs (red triangle), shows a dark box reading '33 supervisors from 17 developers', and lists four metrics. 02 Use cases lists three deployment settings: input moderation, output moderation, and jailbreak plus prompt injection. 03 Taxonomies shows the harm taxonomy (11 categories) and the jailbreak taxonomy (13 techniques) as white boxes. 04 Datasets gives four dataset boxes with sample counts and a note on paraphrasing. 05 Framework has a dark 'BELLS-O' orchestration box that runs both API and local supervisors. 06 Results shows a small scatter plot with a dashed green 'best' region and a dark 'Public leaderboard' box. The eye lands first on the dark boxes and the numbered headings.
caption: BELLS-O benchmark pipeline. We evaluate 33 supervision systems from 17 developers, spanning the major specialized guardrails and a representative slice of frontier LLMs repurposed as supervisors. Systems are scored under a unified harness on three use cases (input and output content moderation, jailbreak and prompt-injection detection) and four operational metrics (detection rate, false-positive rate or FPR, latency, cost). The 11-category harm taxonomy is aligned to the GPAI Code of Practice; synthetic content-moderation samples are paraphrased to suppress generator-specific fingerprints. The released leaderboard exposes the per-use-case Pareto frontier across all four metrics.
abstract: LLM supervision systems, namely input/output moderation filters and jailbreak detectors, are the primary safeguard against misuse in deployed AI applications, yet existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased, omit cost and latency, and rarely compare specialized guardrails against repurposed generalist LLMs. We present BELLS-O (Benchmark for the Evaluation of LLM Supervision Systems, Operational), an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 systems from 17 developers: specialized guardrails (e.g., Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, Lakera Guard) and frontier generalists repurposed as supervisors (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast), jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost. We cover input/output moderation across 11 harm categories, jailbreak detection across 13 attack techniques, and prompt-injection detection, using in-house datasets built from handcrafted prompts, curated external samples, and quality-controlled synthetic generation, with synthetic moderation samples paraphrased to suppress generator fingerprints. Content-moderation runs are repeated five times and all rates reported with 95% intervals. The Pareto frontier reveals use-case-dependent tradeoffs. On content moderation, specialized supervisors are operationally ahead: top systems match the best generalist LLMs on detection (93-96%, no significant difference) at low false-positive rates while running ~5x faster; cost depends more on serving setup than on class. On jailbreak detection, generalist LLMs achieve higher median detection on three of four datasets and lower false-positive rates, but at higher latency and, for closed frontier models, 10-100x higher cost. On prompt injection, the two best dedicated detectors lead. We release the framework, an interactive leaderboard, and four datasets as a vendor-neutral basis for selecting safeguards under deployment constraints.
